title: Grandmother's cornet, Victrola records and the pawn shop in Jacksonville
summary: Tolliver hears Jazz at the Philharmonic 78s, Roy Eldridge, Shavers and Dizzy, sees a cornet in a pawn shop window and his grandmother buys it.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Am I correct that your grandmother, we can thank your grandmother for handing you a cornet?
Can I ask you why you wanted it? What was it that might have been going on in your household or in your neighborhood or on the radio perhaps that made you want to get your hands on that cornet?

Well by the time I was five years old my mom had a genuine Victrola, you know, just like the ones that are in the museum. And she had the Jazz at the Philharmonic recordings by Norman Granz. You know? Pretty hip for that time. And I’d sit myself down and put that big arm on those thick 78s and listening to all of that is what got me to where I am today and I believe it was probably L’il Jazz (Roy Eldridge), and Charlie Shavers, you know, just the sound of the trumpet you know. And of course Dizzy Gillespie. And I guess I was about six or seven or so, you know, just walking through the sandy streets of Jacksonville. You know at that time there were no pavement, there was no asphalt, even for a metropolis town like Jacksonville, certain areas it was just sand you know. And there was this little pawn shop that I would pass every day going from kindergarten back home. And I saw this cornet hanging in the window you know, enticing someone to come
in and get it. And above it was some sheet music of Dizzy Gillespie you know, and I’m saying oh boy, this is right up my alley.
That’s like a message from somewhere.

Yeah. So I said to Grandmama, you know, I sure would like to have that cornet. And you know God bless her, you can imagine, we’re talking 1947, ’48. I don’t know how she saved the pennies but she went and got that thing for me. And the rest is history.
That’s really interesting. And you must have seen some pictures to connect what you were hearing on the 78s to what the instrument was, or maybe you asked around, like what is that sound?

Well I was already in the drum & bugle corps at my grade school, switching me from the bugle to the drums you know, so music was always there in one form or another all the time. So I mean I knew of course what the instrument looked like and sounded like of course. It was a matter of my getting my hands on one that I could have 24/7 you know.
